description: We are a six-frog team from Ukraine. We’ve competed in several hackathons, so we know how to scope tightly, split work cleanly and ship a working demo under pressure. Our strength is turning large, messy datasets into tools people can actually use. We care about validation as much as speed: we test our models against real data and are upfront about what they can and can’t do.
summary:
FieldSense is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers plan crop rotations for a changing climate. It combines NASA Earth observations (such as POWER weather, GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, HLS v2.0 imagery and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections etc.) with other sources like ESA Sentinel-1 radar, the USDA Cropland Data Layer and USDA soil surveys and more.

Our tool enables farmers to explore real-time and historical metrics of each field. Machine-learning and statistical models provide real-time analysis of each field's health and several rotation strategies for consideration. An SI assistant makes our tool customisable for user's priorities and constraints and interpretable for people with any level of technical or geospatial experience, explaining each strategy’s benefits, evidence, gaps and risks. It supports farmers’ judgment and local expertise, not replaces them.
details:
FieldSense's code is available on GitHub. We used Claude Code and Codex for speeding up the development and efficiently debugging functionality.

Problem overview and our solution

Across 16 million analyzed US fields, 1 out of 4 breaks rotation rules. For example, 26% of corn fields and 26% of soybean fields had the same crop sown for two consecutive years.

To make matters worse, climate change is making weather less stable and predictable, and is changing soil water, pest pressure and growing seasons with it. As a result, farmers around the world can no longer make efficient rotation decisions based only on their knowledge of a once stable environment.

There is a critical need for a solution that analyses how temperatures are shifting, discovers patterns and anomalies in rainfalls, water shortages, erosion, nutrient depletion and extreme weather, and helps farmers choose which crops to add to a rotation more efficiently and reliably.

This is exactly the challenge FieldSense addresses. We collected data from more than a dozen data products, used these datasets to train and fine-tune several machine-learning and statistical models, and integrated an SI assistant to make the results interpretable and personal.

FieldSense provides a detailed overview of each field, allowing the farmer to review soil-moisture and soil-depletion metrics, climate-risk analysis, crop history, and a detailed risk analysis for each suggested rotation strategy. The farmer can also track events such as droughts, extreme weather and planned sowings on the built-in calendar. On the Environment page, the farmer can review past, current and future weather, along with its impact on the selected crop.

All the data provided by the platform can be explained and explored further with the integrated SI assistant. You can view the full video demonstration on Google Drive.

FieldSense is built first for farmers, especially row-crop growers who are weighing whether to change a corn–soybean or wheat rotation, add a cover crop or introduce a new crop. No technical or geospatial background is needed, since every result can be explained in plain language.

The same per-field insights also serve the people who advise farmers, such as agronomists, crop consultants, cooperatives and extension services, who can use them to support their recommendations across many farms. Beyond the farm, sustainability programmes, crop insurers, lenders and public conservation agencies can use aggregated, opt-in insights to track practice change and understand climate risk across regions.


Data decisions

After carefully analysing the landscape of available data products, we chose the following:

  • USDA NASS Crop Sequence Boundaries (CSB) with Cropland Data Layer (CDL) crop codes to get the list of about 16 million US fields with their locations and areas, together with each field's crop history for 2018–2025. We use this history to build rotation features, to compare fields with different rotation histories and to label training data for our crop classifier.
  • USDA NASS Quick Stats: county crop yields to get yearly county yields of corn and soybeans, which serve as the target and yield history for our yield model and rule engine, and as an aggregate check on the direction of the effects found by our Neighbour Evidence Engine.
  • USDA NASS Quick Stats: Crop Progress to see how far crop development had progressed in a field's state on any given day. From it we derive the sowing lag, the growing-degree-day constants for mapping crop stages and the harvest date, and we use it to validate our planting and harvest windows year by year.
  • NASA POWER to get daily temperature, humidity, wind, rainfall and solar radiation for each field's weather cell. Its 45-year record (1981–2025) lets us fit sowing, frost and heat windows and their year-to-year variability, and it supplies the weather that drives our off-season soil-water model.
  • NASA GPM IMERG to get satellite rainfall at about 10 km, independent of the POWER reanalysis, along with a per-cell error estimate.
  • NASA SMAP L4 soil moisture to measure daily surface and root-zone soil moisture, which tells us about in-season water stress and helps identify drought seasons. It is also the reference our off-season water model is corrected against, including frozen-soil behaviour in winter, and its leaf area and snow information help us separate bare days from snow-covered ones.
  • NASA Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) v2.0 to follow each field through the season with 30 m vegetation and water indices (NDVI, EVI, NDWI) every 2–3 days. The same data trains our crop classifier and shows how well greenness and plant water held up in drought seasons.
  • NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 to see how temperature and rainfall are expected to shift by around 2040. We use these projections to move planting, frost and heat windows into the future, and the spread between climate models becomes our measure of uncertainty.
  • Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar (Microsoft Planetary Computer) to fill gaps in the optical record, since radar sees through clouds and works at night, and to capture crop structure on the same seasonal timeline as the optical data.
  • gridMET to get 4 km daily weather and reference evapotranspiration, which POWER does not provide, and to calibrate evapotranspiration in our water model.
  • NOAA Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI) to get a weekly, physically based drought signal that responds earlier than drought maps and does not depend on rainfall.
  • U.S. Drought Monitor to assign each field weekly expert-assessed drought classes, which we use to decide which seasons count as drought seasons.
  • USDA RMA Cause of Loss to get crop-insurance payouts by county, cause and year. This gives an independent record of drought, heat and excess-moisture years, which we use to validate drought seasons and label crop stress.
  • USDA NRCS gSSURGO / gNATSGO soil survey to get each field's soil properties: available water storage, drainage, slope, organic matter, texture and depth to the water table. These drive our water and stress rules and let us compare fields fairly by accounting for differences in their soils.

Data collection

The work happened in four stages. To start with, we created a single base layer of farm fields. On the next step, every external data source was collected on its own, into its own folder and table. Those separate tables were then joined into the datasets that the machine-learning models actually read. The joined pilot datasets were extended with further sources and longer histories, since we didn't have to rebuild anything that already existed we managed to significantly save time and resources on additional data collection.

Everything started with the USDA NASS Crop Sequence Boundaries. The ingest step read the geodatabase in fixed-size batches and wrote them as Parquet files. A few optional helpers work on top of this base layer. For example, estimated bounding box built for each field from its centre and area, exact polygons extracted from the geodatabase for a chosen state or county, inside point a point guaranteed to lie inside each polygon used by frontend and new crop years when a newer Cropland Data Layer year is released, the national CDL GeoTIFF can be sampled at each field and the result added as a new crop-code column to a copy of the batches.

Then we collected individual datasets from each of the selected data products.

Weather, satellite rainfall and soil moisture

Daily weather comes from NASA POWER through its public REST API at power.larc.nasa.gov. The collector first works out which POWER grid cells cover the fields, then sends one request per cell centre to the daily point endpoint and merges the answers. POWER marks gaps with the value −999, and these are stored as missing values rather than numbers so that they cannot distort averages later. The result is a map from each field to its weather cell, a weather_daily.parquet table and a small units.json file recording the units POWER reported. The same cells were later extended back to 1981 to give a 45-year record.

Satellite rainfall comes from GPM IMERG and is collected with NASA's earthaccess Python library. IMERG is distributed as one global file per day, which is far more than we need, so the collector handles it one day at a time. It finds that day's file in NASA's CMR catalogue, downloads it, reads only the cells it planned to use and then deletes the file. This keeps disk use low allowing us to minimaze costs for storage and compute. The output is again a field-to-cell map, together with daily data in Parquet format.

Soil moisture comes from the SMAP Level 4 product SPL4SMGP, also through earthaccess, from the NSIDC data centre. Because downloads from NSIDC are not always reliable, the collector tries three routes in turn: a bulk download after a CMR search, then a file-by-file download, and finally a manual download through the logged-in session. The HDF5 files sit on the EASE-Grid 2.0 grid and are read with h5py. SMAP delivers eight three-hourly files per day, which are averaged into one daily value per cell, producing a field-to-cell map and daily data in Parquet format.

Drought, yields and soil

The U.S. Drought Monitor publishes one drought map per week, valid on Tuesdays. The collector downloads these weekly maps as shapefiles or GeoJSON from the NDMC website and caches them locally, then checks which drought polygon contains each field's centre to find its drought class. The result is a long table with one row per field and week, holding the field ID, the map's valid date, the drought class and an estimated release date.

County yields come from the NASS Quick Stats REST API in JSON format, authenticated with an API key. Quick Stats returns at most 50,000 rows per request, so large requests are split up, first by range of years and then state by state, until each piece fits under the limit. When working offline, a CSV exported from the Quick Stats website can be used instead.

Soil properties come from the USDA gSSURGO and gNATSGO soil surveys through the Soil Data Access web service, which accepts SQL queries over HTTPS. For each field the collector first looks up the soil map unit at the field's location, then queries the muaggatt, component and chorizon tables for that unit's properties. A faster optional route samples a local copy of the gNATSGO map-unit raster instead of querying the service point by point. The outputs are a parquet file with one row per field, a parquet file with county summaries and a small cache of map-unit keys so that repeated runs do not query the same locations again.

Satellite time series of the fields

Optical imagery comes from NASA's Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) version 2.0, which combines the Sentinel-2 product HLSS30 and the Landsat product HLSL30 on one 30 m grid. Images are found through earthaccess and the CMR catalogue. Instead of downloading whole scenes, the collector reads only the small window around each field from the Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, either through the authenticated session or through GDAL with a bearer token. For every field and date it keeps the average NDVI, EVI and NDWI over the pixels inside the field that the Fmask cloud mask marks as clear.

Even reading windows, HLS for all fields would be too large a download, so the search is limited to the sample of fields used in the project. Images are searched cell by cell and thinned to a few per time step, which keeps the seasonal picture of each field while skipping most of the redundant granules.

Radar imagery from Sentinel-1 fills the gaps that clouds leave in the optical record. It comes from Microsoft Planetary Computer through its STAC API and the sentinel-1-rtc collection, again read window by window, with an anonymous access token fetched automatically. The VV and VH backscatter values are converted to decibels and placed on the same 16 time steps as the optical data, so that both can be used together. Finally, for quick lookups at a given point, Sentinel-2 Level-2A imagery is read through the Element84 Earth Search STAC API, which serves files from AWS without needing an account. This returns the latest greenness at that location.

Final datasets preparation

In this stage the separate tables collected previously are joined into the datasets that the models actually read. Two keys hold everything together are the field-to-cell maps, which link each field to its weather, rainfall and soil-moisture cells, and the county key, which links fields to county yields and county summaries.

The first step builds county and weather features. For every county and year, the share of each crop and of each rotation is computed from the crop-code columns, weighted by field acreage. The daily cell tables from POWER, IMERG and SMAP are then summarised over defined time windows of the season. For county-level work these summaries are weighted by the acres of fields falling in each cell, while for the per-field datasets they are kept per cell and year. Drought features follow the same logic. For each year, the collector picks the latest Drought Monitor map published by a chosen as-of date and records either the share of each county's area in drought or the drought class of each individual field.

The main dataset has one row per field per year. It is built in DuckDB one year at a time and joins each field's ID and coordinates, its own crop history, the weather and drought features, its soil properties and the county yield, which serves as the label. Because that yield is a county figure, every field in a county carries the same value. The output is written in year partitions. Alongside it sits a per-field daily dataset with one row per field, per candidate crop and per day within a single year. Each row carries the weather of the field's cells and the drought class from the latest map released on or before that day, so that no row ever sees information from its own future. This dataset is written as one file per county.

For the crop classifier, the per-observation satellite tables are turned into regular time-series tensors. The season is divided into 16 equal time steps, each step takes the median of the observations that fall within it, and empty steps are filled by linear interpolation. The channels are NDVI, EVI and NDWI, plus VV and VH backscatter when Sentinel-1 is used. The data is split into training, validation and test sets by county, and the result is written together with the tensors, in one folder per year.

The Neighbour Evidence Engine has its own analysis table. It combines the CSB field attributes, the composed HLS tables (with the same list of fields in every year), the weekly Drought Monitor table, the soil data, POWER and SMAP, and the county yields. Working through the rows in batches, it reduces the 32 tensor columns to five outcome measures and writes one row per field per year, which can be reused on later runs without rebuilding.

One rule applies to every model trained on these datasets. Because the label is a county value shared by all fields in that county, models are always validated by splitting on year, and additionally on county to test how well they transfer to new places. They are never validated by splitting fields within the same county and year, since those fields share the same label and such a split would make the model look far more accurate than it really is.


Data pipeline architecture

Machine learining and statistical models

TempCNN

TempCNN determines which crop was grown on a field in a given season. The model looks at how the greenness and water content of the crop changed over the season and assigns the field to one of the classes: corn, soybeans, alfalfa, grassland/pasture or "Other". Classification is run for every field that SAM 2 finds inside the area selected by the user. Satellite data for the season are downloaded for each field and the crop is determined from them alone; we do not look up crop history in any additional source.

The model receives a tensor of 5 channels by 16 time steps for one field in one season. Three channels (NDVI, EVI and NDWI) are calculated from HLS optical data, and the other two (VV and VH) are Sentinel-1 radar backscatter. The season is divided into 16 equal intervals, the median of the observations is taken for each one, and gaps are filled by linear interpolation. This way radar compensates for cloudy periods, when optical imagery shows nothing. VV values (from −30 to 5 dB) and VH values (from −35 to 0 dB) are scaled to the range 0 to 1 so that the scale of the radar does not outweigh the indices. The same normalisation is applied at inference as in training.

The architecture is a one-dimensional convolutional network that treats the time series as a sequence. Three Conv1D blocks with kernel size 5 (128, 256 and 256 filters), each followed by BatchNorm and ReLU, look for characteristic development phases: the rise in greenness after sowing, the peak of the growing season, and the decline at ripening or cutting. Global average pooling then collapses the series into a vector of 256 features, Dropout of 0.5 guards against overfitting, and a linear layer outputs logits for four classes.

The training set contains 7,921 fields, about 2,000 per class. Labels come from the CDL codes in the CSB table: 1 for corn, 5 for soybeans, 36 for alfalfa and 176 for grassland/pasture. The classes are nearly balanced, so class imbalance does not distort training. The data are split in a stratified way 80/10/10 into training, validation and test sets. We used the Adam optimiser (learning rate 5·10⁻⁵, L2 regularisation 10⁻⁴), cross-entropy loss, a batch size of 64 and 50 epochs. The learning rate is halved if the validation loss does not improve for three epochs in a row. The checkpoint with the lowest validation loss is saved, and training can be resumed from it when new data arrive.

On the held-out test set the accuracy was 92.8%. According to the confusion matrix, the share of correctly identified fields is 0.95 for corn, 0.95 for soybeans, 0.93 for grassland/pasture and 0.88 for alfalfa. The only notable error concerns alfalfa. The model mistakes 10% of such fields for grassland. This is expected, since both are perennial crops that stay green for most of the season and produce similar NDVI curves. Accuracy on the training set is about 96% and on the validation set about 93–94%, and the validation loss is stable.

Rejection of low-confidence predictions. The network is trained on four crops, but a user may select a field with any other crop, or a plot with no crop at all. If we relied on softmax probabilities alone, the model would still name one of the four, because the probabilities always sum to one. For this reason, at inference an energy score is calculated for every field, that is, the logarithm of the sum of the exponentials of the logits (logsumexp). It is high for a time series the network recognises and drops for an unfamiliar one, because the logits are small. If the score falls below the threshold of 1.1225, the field is assigned the class "Other", even if one of the probabilities is formally the largest. The threshold was chosen on the basis of an experiment in which we compared the model's confidence on a range of examples; 1.1225 proved optimal because it filters out the largest number of non-target plants while keeping the largest number of target ones. The network itself remains a four-class model. The "Other" class was not trained and required no additional labels. Along with the class, the service returns the probabilities for the four crops and the value of the energy score.

The splits are random by field, so accuracy in new counties and states may be lower. Before the model goes into production it should be checked with a county-level split, as we do for the other models. The accuracy of 92.8% was measured for four classes, without the "Other" class.

SAM 2

SAM 2 (Segment Anything Model 2 from Meta) finds the boundaries of fields in the area the user has selected on the map. On the website the user outlines an area with the "lasso" tool, and the model uses the satellite image to determine the boundaries of the fields inside it, based on colour, texture and the lines that separate a field from its neighbours, from roads and from buildings. Outlines do not have to be drawn by hand, and any plot can be analysed without waiting for ready-made data on it. Satellite data are then downloaded for each field found, and TempCNN determines the crop.

We use the lightest version, SAM 2 Hiera-Tiny. It runs fast on a single GPU, which suits an interactive mode where the response is needed within seconds. We did not fine-tune the model, so it uses pretrained weights and ready configuration.

The process has three steps. First, the whole image passes through the Hiera encoder and is turned into a feature map. This is the heaviest step, and it is performed once per image. Then the area selected by the user is passed to the prompt encoder. Finally, the mask decoder combines the feature map with the prompt and returns a binary mask for each field inside the area. We switched off the multi-mask mode so that each object gets exactly one answer. Together with the mask, the model returns a confidence score, and the mask itself is overlaid on the image as a semi-transparent layer.

The mask shows only the outline of a field, not its crop. This is how the two modules share the work: SAM 2 answers the question "where is the field", and TempCNN answers "what is growing on it".

Neighbour Evidence Engine (CropTwin Detective + CausalSoil)

The Neighbour Evidence Engine answers one practical question - among fields like mine, did those with a different rotation history hold up better in past drought years, and what does that mean for my field? It builds on a simple observation. Weather is the main driver of drought stress, and fields that sit close together share the same weather. If two neighbouring fields grow the same crop in the same year, but one has a monoculture history and the other a diverse rotation, then a difference in how green and well-watered their canopies stay during a drought is evidence about the effect of the rotation itself. By comparing fields only within a 20 km square and a single year, the engine holds weather fixed by design instead of trying to model it.

Each comparison looks at one field in one season, for corn or soybeans separately. The engine tests five rotation practices - continuous cropping versus rotation, a diverse rotation of three or more crop groups versus a narrow one, the presence of small grain or hay in recent years, winter cover versus a bare winter, and a longer gap before the same crop returns. Field condition is measured from satellite time series, such as peak greenness, canopy water content in July–August, late-season greenness and cumulative greenness over the season. A season counts as a drought season when the field's location was in drought class D2 or worse for at least four weeks in July–August, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. The key quantity is the drought-specific effect, which answers how much the gap between the two practices changes when drought arrives, compared with normal years. Soil properties, field size, location and the field's greenness in earlier years are taken into account so that like is compared with like.

To avoid relying on any single method, three estimators are run for every combination of crop, practice and outcome. Matching pairs each treated field with its most similar neighbour. Double machine learning uses gradient-boosting models, with cross-validation folds drawn by 20 km square so that neighbours never act as their own controls. A causal forest estimates how the effect varies with soil water capacity, drought intensity and field size, and produces a field-specific estimate with a 95% interval. The results then go through a series of checks. For instance, whether the compared groups are balanced and overlap, whether shuffling the labels makes the effect disappear, whether a "negative control" (greenness before the practice could have acted) correctly shows no effect, whether the outcome actually responds to drought at all, and whether county yields move in the same direction. Agreement between the methods and the checks is itself part of the evidence.


The engine produces two kinds of answers. At the population level it reports, for each practice, its effect in normal and drought seasons with confidence intervals and a plain verdict (supported, a possible artefact, no detectable effect, or abstain when there is not enough data). At the field level it gives a what-if estimate - the likely drought-season effect of switching to a practice on this particular field, given its own soil and size, together with the number of comparable fields nearby that support it. When there are too few comparable fields, the engine says "insufficient evidence" rather than offering a number.

Every result is labelled as an adjusted association from observational satellite data, not a proven causal effect, and its limits are stated alongside it. Unrecorded management choices such as hybrid, nitrogen rate, tillage or planting date can bias the estimates; greenness and water indices are signs of stress rather than yield; crop labels from national maps can be wrong; and the number of drought seasons in recent years is small, so drought-specific findings rest on only a few seasons. A valid run needs the same fields observed in every year, many fields in both groups within each square and year, at least three seasons including drought years, and enough crop history to define the rotation practices.

Window Forecaster (ChronoShift + Fallow-Zero)

The Window Forecaster answers two timing and water questions that decide whether a rotation or a cover crop is workable on a given field. The first part, ChronoShift, asks when the frost, sowing and heat windows fall at a location today and around 2040, and whether the most sensitive stage of a crop, such as corn silking, is likely to coincide with extreme heat. The second part, Fallow-Zero, asks whether growing a cover crop between harvest and the next sowing makes it more likely that the next crop starts the season short of soil water, compared with leaving the field bare, and how much autumn rain the cover crop needs to be safe. Both answers give date ranges and probabilities built from decades of weather, not a single prediction.

ChronoShift works on weather cells, so all fields in a cell share its results. From NASA POWER daily weather since 1981, it reads off each year's last spring frost, first autumn frost, first workable sowing day and run of hot days, giving a 45-year series for every event. A gradient-boosted quantile model then predicts the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile of each date from the trend and the climate state, and it is kept only if it beats a simple baseline of linear trend plus climatology. To look ahead to about 2040, the observed record is shifted by the monthly temperature and rainfall changes projected by several NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models and two emission scenarios, and the windows are recomputed; the disagreement between models becomes the measure of uncertainty. Growing degree days, calibrated on NASS Crop Progress statistics, place each crop's flowering and grain-fill stages on the calendar, which gives the probability that the sensitive stage overlaps hot days and an adaptation margin such as "tolerates 10–15 days later sowing".

Fallow-Zero runs a daily FAO-56 soil-water balance for each field from harvest to the next spring sowing, in two branches - bare fallow and a cover crop such as cereal rye with its own water use and termination date. The ledger is driven by POWER weather, IMERG rainfall and gridMET reference evapotranspiration, bounded by the soil's available water storage from gSSURGO. A residual model learns the gap between the ledger and SMAP root-zone soil moisture, anchoring it to satellite observation, with leaf area used to identify bare days and snow data used to exclude snow-covered days from calibration. Every historical weather year is then replayed as a scenario, giving the probability that next spring's crop starts below a plant-available-water threshold under each branch, and the autumn rainfall above which the cover crop stays within an acceptable risk.

Both components share one weather record. ChronoShift turns it into event windows and crop-timing risks, and Fallow-Zero turns it into off-season water risk for each field.

Rule engine

The rule engine answers the question a farmer actually asks: "I want to plant this crop on my field - what are my alternatives, and what are the risks of my current rotation?" It turns agronomic knowledge, the field's crop history, regional timing and weather records into a ranked list of candidate crops. Every score can be traced to the rules that produced it. Its rules are written down, sourced and open to inspection, so an agronomist can read, challenge and tune them. This is what the crop recommendation and strategy pages show, and the SI assistant explains its output.

![Rule engine architecture](rule_engine_architecture.png)

Inputs

The engine takes a field (its declared crop, area, location, county and the Crop Sequence Boundaries ID that links it to its satellite-estimated crop history for 2018–2025), the crop the farmer intends to grow and, optionally, priorities: water, soil, erosion, income or pest break. Farmers can also declare practices for the coming season - tillage, tile drainage, a cover crop and its termination date, herbicides used and weed escapes - and soil properties from the USDA soil survey can be added (slope, drainage class, available water storage, sand, pH, carbonates, land capability class and highly-erodible-land status). Whatever is not provided stays silent: a rule that needs missing data does not fire and the gap is listed in the result, so the engine never infers a tillage system or a herbicide programme from satellite data.

Crop catalog and rules

Crops are described in a catalog by group (warm-season grain, small grain, grain legume, perennial forage legume, hay and pasture, fallow and others) and by traits such as plant family, nitrogen fixation, nitrogen demand, water demand, erosion cover factor, months of bare soil, minimum years before the same crop returns and host pests. A candidate list is built for each state from the crops that cover a meaningful share of its acres. The 68 rules are kept in plain YAML files by theme. For example, pests and diseases, soil nutrients, soil properties, erosion and diversity, water and temperature, tillage and residue, weeds and herbicide plant-back, cover crops and double cropping, and yield and market. A rule selects the crops, groups or traits it applies to and states its conditions over facts such as the crop grown last year, the number of years the same crop or family has been repeated, the number of crop groups in the last five years, the county's share of insurance claims for drought, heat, freeze or excess moisture in the previous year and the field's soil. Each rule carries its evidence strength (strong, moderate or weak), its sources and a flag when it needs local review. Rules contain no prose, so the interface and the assistant write the wording and adapt it to the farmer.

Weather hazards counted over decades

Some rules are timed hazards. They ask whether the weather crossed a threshold in a window around a crop stage, for example days above 35 °C around flowering. The engine checks every past season rather than one forecast. It reads a 30-year record (1996–2025) of weekly gridMET statistics on a quarter-degree grid, using the node nearest to the field, and counts in how many seasons the threshold was crossed. The share of seasons hit sets the level of the risk (low, medium or high). A hazard hit in fewer than one season in ten is not reported, and when only the field's own few seasons are available the level is capped at medium. Stage dates (planting, emergence, flowering, grain fill, maturity, harvest) come from the median day each stage reached 50% in USDA NASS Crop Progress for the state, and the local sowing date can move the following stages by the same number of days.

Scoring

Each candidate gets a risk score, where lower is better. A risk adds points by level (low 1, medium 2, high 3), a benefit subtracts a point and an advisory adds nothing. When the farmer picks a priority, the rules in the matching categories count double, so a water priority makes water and temperature findings weigh twice as much. With the income priority, candidates are also ranked by estimated gross revenue and the best-paying one receives a bonus of up to two points; a crop without a price gets no bonus, but no penalty either, and it loses ties. Each candidate's score is broken down by rule and the weights are returned with the result, so the ranking can always be explained from its parts.

Yield, revenue and soil indicators

For each candidate the engine estimates a low, mid and high yield from the county yield trend (corn and soybeans) or from the state range reported by USDA NASS, adjusted by the factors of the rules that fired. Multiplied by the latest marketing-year price received it gives a gross revenue estimate. It is gross only, with no costs, and prices and yields that are not local or not verified are flagged. Soil indicators are derived from crop traits, the crop history and, where available, SMAP root-zone moisture.

Off-season slot

Separately from the ranking, the engine asks what can be done between harvest of the crop now in the field and the next sowing. It opens the slot a week after the median harvest day and tests each option in every season of the weather record. A cereal rye cover crop needs 130 degree days before the year ends, a winter-killed oat cover crop needs 40 days before the first freeze of −2 °C, and winter wheat for harvest needs 400 degree days. An option is reported as reliable when the criterion held in at least 80% of past autumns, marginal from 50% and unlikely below that. The slot never changes scores or ranks.

What the result contains.

For every candidate the result lists the score and its breakdown, the risks, benefits and advisories as structured findings (each with the rule, its conditions or per-season hazard record, evidence strength and level), the sowing calendar, the yield and revenue estimates, soil indicators and the data gaps. At the top level it adds the crop history used and whether it is satellite-estimated, the weather record used, the off-season options and the scoring weights. The planting calendar and the multi-year plan on the strategy pages are built from the same result. The following crop is found by running the engine a second time with the next crop added to the field's history.

Explaining a recommendation

The assistant can ask for an explanation on top of the result, without any change to the scoring. The why part shows which rules added or removed points for the top crop and for the crop the farmer intends to grow, the facts or weather record that triggered each rule (for example three years of corn in a row against a limit of one, or a threshold crossed in 7 of 30 past seasons), its evidence strength and literature references, and where the two crops differ. The method part describes the algorithm step by step with the weights that were actually used, and its limits. The sources part lists the public data sources (USDA CDL and CSB, gridMET, NASS Quick Stats, SSURGO, SMAP, the U.S. Drought Monitor and RMA) and the rule references behind the answer, and the assistant is told to cite only the sources the tool returns.

Multi-year planner

A planning layer on top of the engine chooses a sequence of crops, tillage systems (conventional, strip till, no-till) and cover crops over several years, because each choice changes what the rules say about the next one. It is modelled as a decision problem. The reward is revenue minus production cost, a risk penalty taken from the engine's points and the value of soil carbon, and each step draws one whole historical year (1981–2025), so weather, yields and prices keep their real correlation; the odds of the next year depend on the drought class and the price level just experienced. The exact plan is solved by dynamic programming, and a single network trained with PPO plans for any field in milliseconds. On 1,110 fields in counties held out of training, the learned policy closed 91% of the gap between the year-by-year rule and the exact optimum. The planner currently covers corn, soybeans, oats and alfalfa, the crops with a cost budget, and its cost tables and soil-carbon parameters come from the literature rather than from calibration to these fields.

Honest limits

The engine is built to be cautious about what it claims, and these limits are stated with its results:

  • Crop history comes from satellite maps and can be wrong; it is not a farm record.
  • The weather record is the past, not a forecast, and has no correction for warming. Stage dates are regional medians, so only the sowing date can be local.
  • Corn and soybean yields are county averages; some crops have a placeholder yield or no price and therefore no revenue.
  • Without priorities, the score measures agronomic risk only, so low-input crops such as hay rank first. The income priority or a comparison among cash crops gives a more practical view.
  • Rule thresholds were written for the Corn Belt and have not been reviewed in other regions. Herbicide plant-back intervals are label maxima, and the product label always governs.
  • The off-season check covers autumn heat only, not soil water at seeding, winter survival or spring termination.

SI assistant capabilities

The SI assistant is how a farmer talks to everything above. It does not hold a copy of the data and does not answer from memory about the user's field, so the language model decides which question needs which data, calls the matching tool, reads the result and explains it in plain language. Data is fetched only when an answer needs it, usually one or two tools per question, and general farming questions are answered directly. The answer streams to the screen word by word, with a short progress line such as "Checking soil moisture…" while a tool runs.

To optimize token usage and minimaze the llm hallusinations, we developed 9 SI agent tools. Each tool wraps a service that the web app already uses, so the assistant and the pages always show the same up-to-date numbers. Avaliable tools:

  • Weather forecast. Three days of weather with crop-risk alerts (frost, heat, heavy rain, wind), starting from the forecast day the user has open.
  • Climate timing and risk. Typical sowing, harvest and frost windows and heat and frost risk, as early, median and late dates built from decades of weather and climate projections.
  • Neighbour evidence. Whether neighbouring fields with a different rotation held up better in drought years, always described as an adjusted association from satellite data, with its verdict and limits.
  • Soil moisture. Modelled soil moisture by layer at the field point, optionally compared with the same time of year in past years.
  • Soil depletion. The soil depletion screening index, with the signals behind it.
  • Rotation advice. The ranked next-crop advice from the rule engine, with the risks, benefits and advisories behind each score, so that the assistant can explain why a crop ranks where it does, compare crops or re-rank them for the user's priorities (water, soil, erosion, income, pest break).
  • Calendar events. The events planned on a day or short range: rotation dates calculated from the strategy and warnings about drought (U.S. Drought Monitor), heatwaves, thunderstorms, extreme rain, strong wind and hard frost.
  • Crop production. What the field, or a county or state, produced in a past year according to USDA NASS: the field's area times the county-average yield, or published production totals for a region.
  • Crop revenue. Expected gross revenue (low, base, high) and return on investment of a crop plan, from NASS yield trends and prices received.

New models and data producing functions can be registered as tools without changing the assistant.

Where the farmer meets it

  • Field assistant. A chat for the selected field, with suggested questions such as "Is there a frost risk this week?" or "How depleted is this soil?".
  • Environment page. Each forecast day has a short summary. The farmer can open "Ask a follow-up" under it and ask, for example, whether the day is good for field work or what to watch for in the next days. The assistant knows which day is open.
  • Calendar page. Selecting a day opens a panel on the right. The assistant first explains each event of that day in more detail: what to do, why it falls on that date, what to prepare and what could change it. The farmer can then ask follow-up questions, and the assistant can use any of the tools above, for example to check whether the weather suits the planned work. The panel also lists the day's actions, which the farmer can accept or decline; the choice is saved with the field's calendar.

Strategy and calendar integration

The calendar events come from the same rotation strategy that the strategy pages show. Harvest of the current crop, autumn cover-crop seeding, sowing of the next crop and the crop after it are placed on dates taken from the median of past seasons, and they are joined by forecast and drought warnings. The assistant reads these events through a tool and can go on to explain the strategy behind them with the rotation-advice tool and to put numbers on a plan with the crop-revenue tool.

Guardrails

  • Evidence, not invention.The assistant explains rankings only from the findings a tool returns. When a source has no data, the tool says so and the assistant tells the user instead of guessing. When tools disagree, it says so.
  • Honest labels. Rotation dates are described as typical ranges, not predictions, and warnings as forecast risks, not confirmed damage. Crop history is called satellite-estimated, not a farm record. Production and revenue are labelled as estimates built from county averages and past years, never as harvest records or insurance figures. Neighbour evidence is never presented as a proven effect and, when it abstains, the assistant says that the evidence is too weak to recommend anything.
  • Locked instructions. The system prompt lives on the server and cannot be set or changed by the client. Tool results and field data are treated as data, never as instructions, so text hidden in a field name or a data source cannot redirect the assistant.
  • Privacy and control. The conversation is sent with each request and is not stored by the server. Tools only read data of the signed-in user's own fields.
  • Supports judgment. The assistant offers one or two useful next questions and leaves the decision with the farmer, in line with the aim of supporting local expertise, not replacing it.

Business model and monetization

While farmers benefit most from using our tool, we acknowledge that they are the hardest to charge because of thin margins and free tools such as OneSoil. For this reason, we plan to make our tool free for farmers and paid for by the organisations around them.

We have identified six potential revenue streams:

  1. Advisor and co-op licences (agronomists, crop consultants, cooperatives, extension services). Our tool turns hours of data gathering into minutes and adds an evidence base to their advice.
  2. Sustainability programme verification (food and beverage companies, grain buyers, programme operators). Many companies have supply-chain targets and already pay for verification of practice change, so they are likely to allocate budget to a tool that tracks rotation diversity, cover-crop adoption and the reduction of bare months.
  3. Risk analytics (crop insurers, ag lenders). Our tool will help them price portfolio risk more accurately and develop incentive programmes for resilient practices.
  4. Grants and public partnerships (USDA, e.g. SBIR and conservation programmes; NASA Applied Sciences / NASA Acres; state agencies). FieldSense helps farmers plan practices that public programmes already promote.
  5. API / integration licence (farm management software and ag-tech platforms). Our field calendar, strategy comparison and explanations will let them add rotation planning without building their own data pipeline.
  6. Farmer Pro tier (larger farms). With add-ons such as scenario sliders, alerts, field-boundary uploads and farm-software integration, we can offer convenience at scale while the core tool stays free.
